title: Charlie Parker's troubles and breaking addictions
summary: Parker came to him in trouble, and Barefield reflects on how hard it is to break habits, citing his alcoholic brother and daughter and quitting smoking, and Parker's bitten tongue.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: And Bird -- well, he used to come to see me all the time, you know, because he was in trouble, you know, and I was trying to help him get himself straightened up, but it's hard for a person to -- that's weak -- to get straightened out. I've had several things with different people. I have an alcoholic brother and an alcoholic daughter, and I know how hard it is for these people to break away from things.

And it's hard for a person like me to see why they can't, but I can understand it, because I've never -- oh, I remember -- I never smoked until I was 35, when I went to work at the radio station. Well, it was 32. I was about 32 years old. Then I started to smoke. Well, I smoked for about ten years. But when I got ready to quit, I remember I quit, and
then I started again, I'd quit and I'd start, and one day I just stopped and I never did it again and had -- I had overcome the craves for it, and that was it. Now it's offensive to me.
So but you have -- it's a certain point, your breaking point that you have to go through to break off from something, you know, and some people just can't do it, I imagine.

So that was probably -- that was Bird. Charlie -- Charlie Parker wanted to break away from the things. He was in pretty bad shape. I mean he -- but he just -- in fact, one time he showed me where he had bitten off half of his tongue, had one of those seizures or something and just bit one half of his tongue off from the middle on down to the side.
